domain: Section 3: Ensuring the successful operation of a cloud solution

questions.title: Who deleted the VM yesterday
questions.summary: Who did what and when is an admin activity audit log question.
questions.question: You must determine which user deleted a specific VM instance yesterday afternoon. Where should you look?

options.A: A new Cloud Asset Inventory feed for Compute Engine instances.
options.B: The billing export to BigQuery.
options.C: Admin Activity audit logs in Cloud Logging.
options.D: A Cloud Asset Inventory search across the project.

explanation.summary: Who did what and when is an audit-log question: Admin Activity logs record the principal and the API call, which asset inventory does not.

option_breakdown.A: A feed reports changes from now on; yesterday's deletion has already happened.
option_breakdown.B: Billing data shows spend, not who called an API.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Who did what and when is an audit-log question: Admin Activity logs record the principal and the API call, which asset inventory does not.
option_breakdown.D: Search shows resources that exist now; the deleted VM is gone, and search never shows who acted.

questions.title: Send 10 percent to the new revision
questions.summary: Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage.
questions.question: After validation, 10% of live traffic should go to the new Cloud Run revision while the remainder stays on the old one. What should you do?

options.A: Set the container concurrency on the service.
options.B: Set minimum and maximum instance counts on the service.
options.C: Update the service's traffic split across revisions by percentage.
options.D: Deploy the new revision with a tag and no traffic, then shift traffic explicitly.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage, which is how a gradual rollout is expressed.

option_breakdown.A: Concurrency shapes how many requests each instance handles at once; it does not control which revision serves traffic.
option_breakdown.B: Instance bounds control cold starts and the scaling ceiling; they say nothing about revisions or traffic.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Run splits traffic across revisions by percentage, which is how a gradual rollout is expressed.
option_breakdown.D: Tagging without traffic gives the revision its own URL but sends it no live traffic; the 10% split is still to do.

questions.title: Error rates spike after a release
questions.summary: Previous revisions are retained, so shifting traffic back restores service in seconds.
questions.question: Error rates spike immediately after a Cloud Run release. You need to restore service as quickly as possible, without building or deploying anything. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy a fixed revision with a tag and no traffic.
options.B: Redeploy the previous image as a new revision.
options.C: Lower the container concurrency on the service.
options.D: Route 100% of traffic back to the last good revision.

explanation.summary: Because previous revisions are retained, sending 100% of traffic back to the last good revision restores service in seconds without a rebuild.

option_breakdown.A: A tagged revision with no traffic leaves users on the failing release.
option_breakdown.B: It works, but it deploys a new revision, which the stem rules out and which takes longer than re-pointing traffic.
option_breakdown.C: Concurrency changes load per instance, not the faulty code.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Previous revisions are kept, so sending 100% of traffic back to the last good one restores service in seconds without a rebuild.

questions.title: Connection pool exhausted under load
questions.summary: Lowering container concurrency bounds simultaneous requests, and so connections, per instance.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service opens one database connection per request and begins failing under load with connection-pool exhaustion, although CPU is fine. What should you change?

options.A: Set the container concurrency on the service.
options.B: Raise the maximum number of instances.
options.C: Set a minimum number of instances.
options.D: Raise the CPU limit of each instance.

explanation.summary: Lowering container concurrency reduces the number of simultaneous requests per instance, which directly bounds the connections each instance opens.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Lowering container concurrency reduces the simultaneous requests per instance, which directly caps the connections each instance opens.
option_breakdown.B: More instances don't change how many requests, and so connections, each instance handles at once.
option_breakdown.C: Warm instances help cold starts; each still takes the same number of concurrent requests.
option_breakdown.D: CPU is fine; the limit being hit is connections per instance.

questions.title: Cold starts after idle periods
questions.summary: A minimum instance count keeps containers warm so post-idle requests avoid a cold start.
questions.question: Users complain about latency on the first request after a quiet period. The team accepts paying to keep some capacity warm. What should you change?

options.A: Raise the maximum number of instances.
options.B: Set a minimum number of instances.
options.C: Lower the container concurrency.
options.D: Enable startup CPU boost.

explanation.summary: Setting a minimum number of instances keeps containers warm so requests after idle periods do not pay a cold start.

option_breakdown.A: The maximum caps scale-out; it keeps nothing warm.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A minimum number of instances keeps containers warm, so the first request after a quiet period doesn't wait for a cold start.
option_breakdown.C: Lower concurrency means more instances, and so more cold starts.
option_breakdown.D: CPU boost shortens a cold start but doesn't remove it; the team is willing to pay to avoid cold starts altogether.

questions.title: Pod stuck in Pending
questions.summary: The Events section of describe reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU.
questions.question: A Pod in a GKE cluster has been stuck in Pending for ten minutes, and you need to know why the scheduler won't place it. Which command should you run?

options.A: kubectl logs for the Pod
options.B: kubectl describe pod
options.C: kubectl top pod
options.D: kubectl get pods -o wide

explanation.summary: The Events section of kubectl describe pod reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU or unsatisfied node affinity.

option_breakdown.A: A Pending Pod has never started a container, so there are no logs.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The Events section of kubectl describe pod reports scheduling failures such as insufficient CPU or an unmatched node affinity.
option_breakdown.C: top shows resource usage of running Pods; a Pending Pod has none.
option_breakdown.D: It shows the Pod is Pending and where Pods run, but not why this one can't be scheduled.

questions.title: Stack trace from a crash-looping container
questions.summary: kubectl logs --previous prints output from the terminated container instance.
questions.question: A container in a GKE Pod is restarting repeatedly, and you need the stack trace it printed just before it died. What should you look at?

options.A: The logs of the Pod's current container.
options.B: The Pod's events, from kubectl describe pod.
options.C: The logs of the container's previous, terminated instance.
options.D: The container's restart count in Cloud Monitoring.

explanation.summary: kubectl logs --previous prints the output of the last terminated instance of a container, which is where the fatal stack trace is.

option_breakdown.A: The current instance has just restarted, so its logs start after the crash.
option_breakdown.B: Events show that the container restarted and why it was killed, not what it printed.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The previous instance's logs end with the stack trace it printed before exiting.
option_breakdown.D: The count shows how often it crashes, not why.

questions.title: Roll out a patched image to a Deployment
questions.summary: kubectl set image updates the pod template, triggering a native rolling update.
questions.question: A patched image must be rolled out to a running Deployment without editing and reapplying the manifest by hand. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl rollout restart deployment.
options.B: Scale the Deployment to zero and back up.
options.C: Run kubectl edit deployment.
options.D: Run kubectl set image deployment.

explanation.summary: kubectl set image updates the Deployment's pod template, which triggers Kubernetes' native rolling update.

option_breakdown.A: A restart recreates Pods with the same image.
option_breakdown.B: The Pods come back with the same image, after an outage.
option_breakdown.C: edit opens the manifest in an editor, which is the hand editing the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. kubectl set image updates the Deployment's Pod template, which triggers its rolling update to the new image.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl set image deployment/api api=us-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/repo/api:v2 -n prod

questions.title: Restore the previous Deployment version
questions.summary: kubectl rollout undo re-points the Deployment at its previous ReplicaSet.
questions.question: The image just rolled out is crash-looping and the previous version must be restored immediately, without rebuilding anything. Which command should you run?

options.A: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment.
options.B: Run kubectl rollout restart deployment.
options.C: Run kubectl rollout pause deployment.
options.D: Delete the crash-looping Pods.

explanation.summary: kubectl rollout undo re-points the Deployment at the previous ReplicaSet, which is the fastest restoration path.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. kubectl rollout undo points the Deployment back at the previous ReplicaSet, restoring the old version without a rebuild.
option_breakdown.B: A restart recreates Pods from the same broken template.
option_breakdown.C: Pausing stops further changes; Pods already on the new image stay broken.
option_breakdown.D: The Deployment recreates them from the same broken image.

questions.title: Pre-provision for a known surge
questions.summary: kubectl scale sets the Deployment replica count directly.
questions.question: A predictable traffic surge is expected in an hour and the replica count must be raised ahead of it rather than reactively. Which command should you run?

options.A: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Run kubectl scale deployment.
options.C: Run kubectl rollout restart deployment.
options.D: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.

explanation.summary: kubectl scale sets the Deployment's replica count directly, which is how you pre-provision for a known surge.

option_breakdown.A: An HPA reacts after load rises, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubectl scale sets the Deployment's replica count directly, which pre-provisions for a known surge.
option_breakdown.C: A restart replaces Pods without changing how many there are.
option_breakdown.D: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes for Pods that can't be scheduled; it doesn't add replicas.

questions.title: ImagePullBackOff on GKE nodes
questions.summary: Image pulls use the node pool's service account, which needs Artifact Registry Reader.
questions.question: GKE Pods fail to start with ImagePullBackOff. You confirm the image exists and that the node service account has no Artifact Registry permissions. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to the build service account.
options.B: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.
options.C: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the node pool's service account.
options.D: Grant Storage Object Viewer to the node pool's service account.

explanation.summary: GKE nodes pull images with the node pool's service account, not the Pod's Workload Identity. Grant that service account Artifact Registry Reader on the repository.

option_breakdown.A: Writer allows pushing, which the nodes don't need, and the build account isn't what pulls the image.
option_breakdown.B: The Docker credential helper is for a developer's machine; GKE nodes authenticate as their service account.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Image pulls are made by the kubelet with the node pool's service account, so that identity needs roles/artifactregistry.reader on the repository (or project).
option_breakdown.D: That was the permission for the retired Container Registry's storage buckets; Artifact Registry checks its own roles.

questions.title: Cloud Build cannot push the image
questions.summary: Pushing requires Artifact Registry Writer on the target repository for the build identity.
questions.question: A Cloud Build pipeline builds successfully but fails with a permission error when pushing the resulting image to Artifact Registry. What should you do?

options.A: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.
options.B: Add a gcloud auth configure-docker step to the build.
options.C: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.
options.D: Grant the Artifact Registry Writer role to the build service account.

explanation.summary: Pushing requires the Artifact Registry Writer role on the target repository for the build's service account.

option_breakdown.A: The build gets a permission error, not a missing-repository error.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Build already authenticates as its service account; the error is that the account lacks permission.
option_breakdown.C: Reader allows pulling, not pushing.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Pushing requires the Artifact Registry Writer role on the target repository for the build's service account.

questions.title: Local docker push rejected as unauthenticated
questions.summary: The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host.
questions.question: A developer's local docker push to Artifact Registry is rejected as unauthenticated, even though their gcloud account already holds the Writer role on the repository. What should they do?

options.A: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.
options.B: Grant the developer Artifact Registry Administrator.
options.C: Run gcloud auth login again.
options.D: Create a new repository for the developer.

explanation.summary: The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host before it can present the user's credentials.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The Docker client needs the gcloud credential helper registered for the registry host before it can present the user's credentials.
option_breakdown.B: The developer already has Writer; the push isn't reaching Artifact Registry with any credentials.
option_breakdown.C: gcloud is already signed in; Docker doesn't use those credentials until the helper is configured.
option_breakdown.D: The repository exists, and a new one would reject unauthenticated pushes too.

questions.title: Destination for images near the cluster
questions.summary: A repository with the right format and location must exist before any push.
questions.question: The team is moving its images off the retired Container Registry (gcr.io) and needs a destination for their Docker images located close to their GKE cluster. What should they do first?

options.A: Run gcloud auth configure-docker for the registry host.
options.B: Create an Artifact Registry repository in the required region and format.
options.C: Create a Cloud Storage bucket in the GKE cluster's region.
options.D: Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role to the workload's service account.

explanation.summary: An Artifact Registry repository must exist, with the correct format and location, before any image can be pushed to it.

option_breakdown.A: The credential helper is needed to push from a workstation, but there must be a repository to push to first.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. An Artifact Registry repository must exist, with the correct format and location, before any image can be pushed to it.
option_breakdown.C: Container Registry stored images in buckets; Artifact Registry uses repositories, not buckets you create.
option_breakdown.D: The nodes will need Reader later, but there is nothing to read until a repository exists.

questions.title: Registry storage growing without bound
questions.summary: A cleanup policy deletes versions matching age or count rules automatically.
questions.question: Artifact Registry storage costs have grown steadily because every CI run pushes a new tag and nothing is ever deleted. What should you configure, without writing or scheduling scripts?

options.A: A lifecycle rule on the repository's Cloud Storage bucket.
options.B: Immutable tags on the repository.
options.C: A cleanup policy on the repository.
options.D: A smaller, cheaper storage class on the repository.

explanation.summary: A cleanup policy deletes versions matching age or count rules automatically, which is the managed answer to unbounded artifact growth.

option_breakdown.A: Artifact Registry repositories don't expose a bucket for you to manage.
option_breakdown.B: Immutable tags stop tags being overwritten; they delete nothing.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A cleanup policy deletes versions matching age or count rules automatically, which is the managed answer to unbounded growth.
option_breakdown.D: Artifact Registry has no storage classes to choose between.

questions.title: Add replicas when CPU exceeds 65 percent
questions.summary: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric.
questions.question: A web Deployment must add replicas when average CPU across its Pods exceeds 65%, and remove them when load falls. What should you configure?

options.A: Configure a VerticalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.C: Enable node auto-provisioning on the cluster.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric such as average CPU utilisation.

option_breakdown.A: A VPA changes each Pod's CPU and memory requests, not how many replicas run.
option_breakdown.B: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods can't be scheduled; it doesn't add replicas.
option_breakdown.C: Auto-provisioning creates node pools when needed; it doesn't add replicas either.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales replica count against a target metric such as average CPU utilisation.

questions.title: Pods Pending because the pool is full
questions.summary: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot schedule and removes underused ones.
questions.question: Pods are stuck Pending because the node pool has no spare capacity. The team wants nodes added when needed and removed when idle, automatically. What should you configure?

options.A: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.B: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.
options.C: Set explicit CPU and memory resource requests on the Pods.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled and removes them when they are underused, which is precisely this symptom.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cluster autoscaling adds nodes when Pods can't be scheduled and removes them when they are underused.
option_breakdown.B: A fixed extra pool adds capacity once; nothing adds or removes nodes as demand changes.
option_breakdown.C: Requests tell the scheduler what a Pod needs; they don't add capacity.
option_breakdown.D: An HPA adds replicas, which would only create more Pending Pods.

questions.title: Requests far higher than real usage
questions.summary: The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match.
questions.question: A workload's memory requests on GKE were guessed at deployment and are consistently far above actual usage, wasting the GKE cluster's capacity. What should you configure?

options.A: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
options.B: Configure a VerticalPodAutoscaler.
options.C: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.D: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.

explanation.summary: The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match, which is the remedy for mis-sized requests.

option_breakdown.A: An HPA changes the number of replicas; each replica would keep the oversized request.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The VerticalPodAutoscaler observes real usage and adjusts requests to match, which fixes mis-sized requests.
option_breakdown.C: Cluster autoscaling sizes the node pool to the requests; oversized requests still reserve capacity.
option_breakdown.D: A new node pool adds hardware without changing what each Pod reserves.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f vpa.yaml   # kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler, updateMode: Auto

questions.title: Controlling Autopilot cost per Pod
questions.summary: Autopilot bills on requested resources, so accurate requests are the direct cost lever.
questions.question: On an Autopilot cluster the team is surprised by the bill and wants a direct lever on what they are charged for each Pod. What should they configure?

options.A: Enable cluster autoscaling on the node pool.
options.B: Create an additional node pool with the required machine configuration.
options.C: Set explicit CPU and memory resource requests on the Pods.
options.D: Configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

explanation.summary: Autopilot bills on the resources a Pod requests, so setting accurate requests is the direct lever on cost.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot has no node pools for you to autoscale; Google provisions nodes to fit what Pods request, and you are not billed per node.
option_breakdown.B: Node pools are a GKE Standard concept; on Autopilot you do not create them, and you pay for Pod requests, not for machines.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Autopilot bills on the resources a Pod requests, so setting accurate requests is the direct lever on cost.
option_breakdown.D: An HPA changes the number of Pods; each Pod is still billed for whatever it requests.

questions.title: Local SSD cannot be added in place
questions.summary: Node pool hardware properties are fixed at creation, so new hardware means a new pool.
questions.question: A subset of workloads on a GKE Standard cluster needs nodes with local SSD, and the existing node pool can't be reconfigured in place to provide it. What should you do?

options.A: Add a taint to the existing node pool.
options.B: Resize the existing node pool.
options.C: Enable cluster autoscaling on the existing node pool.
options.D: Create a new node pool with local SSD.

explanation.summary: Node pool properties such as local SSD are fixed at creation, so a new node pool is the only way to introduce different node hardware.

option_breakdown.A: A taint controls which Pods may run on the nodes; it doesn't change their hardware.
option_breakdown.B: Resizing adds more nodes of the same configuration, without local SSD.
option_breakdown.C: The autoscaler adds nodes of the same configuration, without local SSD.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Node hardware such as local SSD is set when a node pool is created, so a new node pool is how you add different node hardware.

questions.title: Six-hourly backups retained two weeks
questions.summary: A snapshot schedule resource policy performs and expires snapshots automatically.
questions.question: A database VM's data disk must be backed up every six hours, with each backup kept for fourteen days, on a managed schedule that needs no scripts. What should you configure?

options.A: A cron job in the VM that runs gcloud compute snapshots create.
options.B: A snapshot schedule attached to the disk.
options.C: Regional Persistent Disk replication for the disk.
options.D: One snapshot of the disk now.

explanation.summary: A resource policy snapshot schedule attached to the disk performs and expires the snapshots automatically on the stated cadence and retention.

option_breakdown.A: It runs automatically, but it is a script someone maintains, and nothing deletes old snapshots.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A snapshot schedule attached to the disk creates snapshots on the cadence and deletes them after the retention period.
option_breakdown.C: Replication keeps a live copy in a second zone; a bad write is replicated too, and there's nothing to restore from.
option_breakdown.D: One snapshot is a single point in time, not a recurring backup.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule db-6h --region=us-central1 \
  --max-retention-days=14 --hourly-schedule=6 --start-time=00:00

questions.title: Safety copy before a risky upgrade
questions.summary: A snapshot captures disk state at that moment and can be restored to a new disk.
questions.question: Before a risky in-place upgrade, the engineer needs a point-in-time copy of the data disk that can be restored if the upgrade fails. What should they create?

options.A: Create a custom image from the configured disk.
options.B: Attach a snapshot schedule resource policy to the disk.
options.C: Create a Persistent Disk snapshot.
options.D: Turn on deletion protection for the VM.

explanation.summary: A snapshot captures the disk's state at that moment and can be restored to a new disk, which is the standard pre-change safety step.

option_breakdown.A: Images are for booting new VMs; for a data disk, a snapshot is the restore point.
option_breakdown.B: A schedule takes snapshots later on its cadence, not one now, before the upgrade.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A snapshot captures the disk at that moment and can be restored to a new disk if the upgrade fails.
option_breakdown.D: It stops the VM being deleted; the upgrade can still corrupt the data.

questions.title: SSH without public IPs or a bastion
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH through Google's frontend to the internal address.
questions.question: Instances have no external IP addresses by organisational policy, yet administrators must still open SSH sessions to them, and the team does not want to run a bastion. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy a bastion host with an external IP and connect through it.
options.B: Enable interactive access to the serial console.
options.C: Connect through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding.
options.D: Enable OS Login and grant the appropriate OS Login IAM role.

explanation.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels the SSH session through Google's frontend to the instance's internal address, so no public IP or bastion is needed.

option_breakdown.A: A bastion works but adds a VM to patch, monitor and secure — unnecessary when IAP provides the same reachability as a managed service.
option_breakdown.B: The serial console recovers an instance whose network stack or sshd is broken; it is not a routine administrative path.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels the SSH session through Google's frontend to the instance's internal address, so no public IP or bastion is needed.
option_breakdown.D: OS Login ties Linux accounts to IAM identities and centralises key management; it is not by itself a network path to an instance without a public address.

questions.title: Instance unreachable after a network change
questions.summary: The serial console works independently of the guest network stack.
questions.question: After an engineer edits the network configuration inside a Linux VM's guest OS, the VM has no network connectivity at all: SSH fails, including through IAP. You need a console prompt on the VM to repair the configuration. What should you do?

options.A: Enable OS Login and grant yourself the OS Login Admin role.
options.B: Connect through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding.
options.C: Add a new SSH key to the instance metadata.
options.D: Enable the interactive serial console and connect to it.

explanation.summary: The interactive serial console is reached through Compute Engine, not the guest's network stack, so it works when the VM's own networking is broken.

option_breakdown.A: OS Login changes who may log in over SSH; SSH still needs the network that is broken.
option_breakdown.B: IAP tunnels to the VM's network interface, which is down inside the guest.
option_breakdown.C: A new key still needs a working network path for SSH.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The serial console doesn't depend on the guest's network, so it gives a login prompt to fix the configuration.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances add-metadata app-1 --zone=us-central1-a \
  --metadata=serial-port-enable=TRUE
gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port app-1 --zone=us-central1-a

questions.title: RDP to a Windows VM without a public IP
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels arbitrary TCP ports, including RDP's 3389.
questions.question: A Windows instance with no external IP must be reachable over RDP by a small group of administrators. What should you do?

options.A: Enable OS Login on the Windows instance.
options.B: Tunnel RDP through IAP TCP forwarding.
options.C: Temporarily attach an external IP whenever an administrator needs access.
options.D: Enable the interactive serial console for the administrators.

explanation.summary: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels any TCP port — here RDP's 3389 — to an instance without a public address, authorised per user by IAM.

option_breakdown.A: OS Login is for Linux accounts, and it is not a network path.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels any TCP port, here RDP's 3389, to a VM without a public address. It needs a firewall rule for 35.235.240.0/20 and the IAP-secured Tunnel User role for the administrators.
option_breakdown.C: An external IP exposes RDP to the internet whenever it is attached.
option_breakdown.D: The serial console is for recovery; it is not a way to run RDP sessions.

questions.title: Promotion with an approval before production
questions.summary: Cloud Deploy models ordered targets with required approvals between stages.
questions.question: A validated release must move through dev, then staging, then production, with a human approval required before production and a record of which release is in each environment. What should you configure?

options.A: Traffic splitting between Cloud Run revisions.
options.B: An Artifact Registry repository per environment.
options.C: A Cloud Build configuration triggered from the repository.
options.D: Use Cloud Deploy to promote the release through a delivery pipeline.

explanation.summary: Cloud Deploy models exactly this: a delivery pipeline with ordered targets and required approvals between stages.

option_breakdown.A: Traffic splitting shifts users between revisions of one service, not a release between environments.
option_breakdown.B: Repositories store images; they don't promote, approve or track releases.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Build runs the build and deploy steps, but it doesn't model ordered environments or show which release each one has.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Cloud Deploy models a delivery pipeline with ordered targets, approvals before a target, and the release running in each.

questions.title: Keep source code off laptops
questions.summary: Cloud Workstations provides managed development environments running in your VPC.
questions.question: Developers waste days configuring laptops, and the security team wants source code to stop living on local machines entirely. What should you provision?

options.A: Cloud Shell for every developer.
options.B: Provision Cloud Workstations for the development team.
options.C: A Compute Engine VM that each developer sets up.
options.D: Full-disk encryption on every laptop.

explanation.summary: Cloud Workstations provides managed, preconfigured development environments running in your VPC, which keeps source off endpoints.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud Shell is a personal, temporary environment with a small home directory, not managed, preconfigured team environments in your network.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Workstations provides managed, preconfigured development environments in your VPC, which keeps source off laptops.
option_breakdown.C: Code moves off laptops, but each developer still spends days configuring a VM.
option_breakdown.D: Encryption protects code on laptops; it doesn't stop code living there or save setup time.

questions.title: Alert on an error string in the logs
questions.summary: A log-based counter metric turns matching entries into a time series an alert can evaluate.
questions.question: The team must alert on the rate of a specific application error that appears only as a string in the service's logs, with no corresponding metric. What should you create?

options.A: Build a Cloud Monitoring dashboard.
options.B: Create an alerting policy on the metric with a notification channel.
options.C: Install and configure the Ops Agent on the instances.
options.D: Create a log-based metric from a Cloud Logging query.

explanation.summary: A log-based counter metric turns matching log entries into a time series that an alerting policy can then evaluate.

option_breakdown.A: A dashboard needs a metric to chart, and it notifies nobody.
option_breakdown.B: There is no metric to alert on yet; the error exists only as log text.
option_breakdown.C: The Ops Agent collects VM metrics and logs; the error string is already in Cloud Logging.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A log-based counter metric turns matching log entries into a time series, and an alerting policy can then watch its rate.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging metrics create payment_errors \
  --log-filter='severity=ERROR AND jsonPayload.event="payment_failed"'

questions.title: Is the site reachable from other continents
questions.summary: Uptime checks probe the endpoint from Google's global checker locations.
questions.question: Management wants to know whether the public website is reachable from several continents, independently of any internal metric. What should you create?

options.A: Create an uptime check against the public endpoint.
options.B: Install and configure the Ops Agent on the instances.
options.C: Create a log-based metric from a Cloud Logging query.
options.D: Deploy Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus.

explanation.summary: Uptime checks probe the endpoint from Google's global checker locations, which is the only option that measures external reachability.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Uptime checks probe the endpoint from checker locations on several continents, which measures external reachability.
option_breakdown.B: The Ops Agent reports from inside the VMs, so it can't say whether users elsewhere can reach the site.
option_breakdown.C: Log-based metrics count what the service logged, which says nothing about requests that never arrived.
option_breakdown.D: Managed Prometheus collects metrics that workloads expose, again from the inside.

questions.title: Keep Prometheus instrumentation without servers
questions.summary: Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes and stores Prometheus metrics as a managed service.
questions.question: Application teams already instrument their GKE workloads with Prometheus client libraries and PromQL dashboards, and want to keep both without running their own Prometheus servers. What should you deploy?

options.A: Self-managed Prometheus servers on the GKE cluster.
options.B: Deploy Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus.
options.C: The Ops Agent's Prometheus receiver on each node.
options.D: Custom metrics written to the Cloud Monitoring API.

explanation.summary: Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes and stores Prometheus-format metrics as a managed service, preserving the existing instrumentation and PromQL.

option_breakdown.A: Running their own Prometheus servers is what the teams want to stop.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes and stores Prometheus-format metrics as a managed service, preserving the existing instrumentation and PromQL.
option_breakdown.C: The Ops Agent is for Compute Engine VMs; GKE nodes are managed by GKE, which has its own managed collection.
option_breakdown.D: The teams would have to re-instrument their code, and they'd lose PromQL dashboards as they are.

questions.title: Alert on p95 request latency
questions.summary: Cloud Run exports latency as a distribution metric with percentile aligners.
questions.question: A team wants to be notified when a Cloud Run service's request latency at the 95th percentile exceeds one second. What should you configure?

options.A: An uptime check against the service URL with a 1-second timeout.
options.B: A dashboard chart of p95 latency that the team checks each morning.
options.C: An alerting policy on the service's request latency at the 95th percentile.
options.D: A log-based metric extracting latency from request logs, with no alerting policy.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run already reports request latency as a distribution; aligning it to the 95th percentile gives the condition, and only an alerting policy notifies anyone.

option_breakdown.A: An uptime check measures reachability from probe locations, not the service's own p95 across all requests.
option_breakdown.B: A dashboard shows the problem to whoever looks; it notifies nobody.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Run already reports request latency as a distribution (run.googleapis.com/request_latencies); an alerting policy aligned to the 95th percentile, with a 1,000 ms threshold and a notification channel, notifies the team.
option_breakdown.D: The metric already exists, and a metric without an alerting policy never notifies.

questions.title: SQL investigation across a year of audit logs
questions.summary: Native BigQuery tables of logs, in a dataset you own, come from a log sink; Log Analytics queries logs in place.
questions.question: From now on, the security team must keep every audit log entry for at least twelve months as native tables in their own BigQuery dataset, in a project they administer, where their scheduled queries join the entries with other tables. What should you configure?

options.A: Create a log sink with a Cloud Storage bucket destination.
options.B: Create a log sink with a Pub/Sub topic destination.
options.C: Configure a log bucket with custom retention and enable Log Analytics.
options.D: Create a log sink with a BigQuery dataset destination.

explanation.summary: A sink to BigQuery copies log entries into native tables in a dataset the team owns, where they are joined and scheduled like any other BigQuery data.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud Storage holds log files, not native tables that scheduled queries can join.
option_breakdown.B: Pub/Sub streams entries to subscribers; nothing lands in BigQuery tables without more work.
option_breakdown.C: Log Analytics queries logs where Cloud Logging stores them, and a linked dataset is a read-only view; it doesn't put native tables in the team's own dataset.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A sink to BigQuery writes log entries as native tables in a dataset the team owns, where they can be joined and queried like any other data.

questions.title: Seven-year retention at lowest cost
questions.summary: A Cloud Storage sink into an Archive-class bucket is the cheapest compliant destination.
questions.question: Regulations require seven years of log retention at the lowest possible cost. Retrieval measured in hours is acceptable. What should you configure?

options.A: A sink to an Archive-class Cloud Storage bucket.
options.B: Configure a log bucket with custom retention and enable Log Analytics.
options.C: A sink to BigQuery, with seven-year table expiration.
options.D: Add an exclusion filter to the _Default sink.

explanation.summary: A Cloud Storage sink with an Archive-class bucket is the cheapest compliant destination for multi-year retention.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A sink to an Archive-class bucket is the cheapest destination for logs kept for years and rarely read.
option_breakdown.B: Log buckets can keep logs for years, but retention in Cloud Logging costs more than Archive storage.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery storage costs more than Archive storage for data that is rarely queried.
option_breakdown.D: An exclusion drops entries, which breaks the retention requirement.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging sinks create archive-sink storage.googleapis.com/log-archive-bucket
# log-archive-bucket uses the ARCHIVE default storage class

questions.title: Stream logs to an on-premises SIEM
questions.summary: A Pub/Sub sink is the supported streaming egress to an external consumer.
questions.question: Log entries must be streamed in near real time to an on-premises SIEM that already consumes a message queue. What should you configure?

options.A: Log Analytics, with a linked BigQuery dataset.
options.B: Create a log sink with a Pub/Sub topic destination.
options.C: Create a log sink with a BigQuery dataset destination.
options.D: Create a log sink with a Cloud Storage bucket destination.

explanation.summary: A Pub/Sub sink is the supported streaming egress from Cloud Logging to an external consumer such as a SIEM.

option_breakdown.A: Log Analytics is for querying logs, not streaming them to an external system.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A Pub/Sub sink is the supported streaming route from Cloud Logging to an external consumer such as a SIEM.
option_breakdown.C: The SIEM would have to poll BigQuery, which isn't streaming and doesn't fit a queue consumer.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Storage sinks write files in batches, about hourly, not in near real time.

questions.title: 400-day retention queried in place
questions.summary: A log bucket with extended retention and Log Analytics allows SQL queries in place.
questions.question: Logs must be retained for 400 days and queried with SQL, without leaving Cloud Logging or paying to store a second copy. What should you configure?

options.A: Create a log sink with a Cloud Storage bucket destination.
options.B: Create a log sink with a Pub/Sub topic destination.
options.C: Configure a log bucket with custom retention and enable Log Analytics.
options.D: Raise the retention of the _Required log bucket.

explanation.summary: A log bucket with an extended retention period and Log Analytics enabled allows SQL queries in place, avoiding a duplicate export.

option_breakdown.A: A Cloud Storage copy is a second copy outside Cloud Logging, and it can't be queried with SQL there.
option_breakdown.B: Pub/Sub streams entries elsewhere; it keeps nothing and runs no SQL.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A log bucket with an extended retention period and Log Analytics enabled allows SQL queries in place, avoiding a duplicate export.
option_breakdown.D: The _Required bucket's retention can't be changed, and it holds only audit and system logs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=400
gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --enable-analytics

questions.title: Reads of table data were never recorded
questions.summary: Admin Activity logs are always on; Data Access logs record reads and must be enabled.
questions.question: An investigation finds that changes to a Cloud Storage bucket's configuration were logged, but reads of its objects were not recorded at all. What should you configure?

options.A: An Admin Activity audit log filter for Cloud Storage.
options.B: A log sink that routes audit logs to BigQuery.
options.C: Log Analytics on the _Required log bucket.
options.D: Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage.

explanation.summary: Admin Activity audit logs are always on, but Cloud Storage Data Access logs, which record object reads, are off by default and must be enabled in the audit configuration.

option_breakdown.A: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes, which are already logged; they never record object reads.
option_breakdown.B: A sink routes entries that exist; reads were never logged, so there is nothing to route.
option_breakdown.C: Log Analytics queries what is stored; it doesn't create missing entries.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Enabling DATA_READ audit logs for Cloud Storage records reads of objects from then on.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID > policy.yaml
# add auditConfigs: service storage.googleapis.com, logType DATA_READ
gcloud projects set-iam-policy PROJECT_ID policy.yaml

questions.title: Health-check log entries dominate cost
questions.summary: An exclusion filter stops those entries being ingested and billed.
questions.question: Logging costs are dominated by high-volume health-check entries that nobody ever reads or needs retained. What should you configure?

options.A: Add an exclusion filter to the _Default sink.
options.B: Shorten the _Default bucket's retention to one day.
options.C: Route the entries to an Archive-class Cloud Storage bucket.
options.D: Log the health checks at a lower severity.

explanation.summary: An exclusion filter on the _Default sink stops those entries being ingested and billed, which is the direct cost remedy.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An exclusion filter on the _Default sink stops those entries being ingested and billed, which is the direct cost remedy.
option_breakdown.B: Most of the cost is ingestion, which shorter retention doesn't reduce.
option_breakdown.C: That keeps entries nobody needs, and they still cost something to store.
option_breakdown.D: Entries at any severity are still ingested and billed.

questions.title: Subnet has run out of addresses
questions.summary: A subnet's primary IPv4 range can be expanded in place with no disruption.
questions.question: A subnet provisioned as a /24 has run out of addresses, and the workloads inside it cannot be migrated elsewhere. What should you do?

options.A: Add a secondary IP range to the subnet.
options.B: Expand the subnet's primary IPv4 range to a larger prefix.
options.C: Reserve static internal addresses for the busiest VMs.
options.D: Shrink a neighbouring subnet to free its addresses.

explanation.summary: A subnet's primary IPv4 range can be expanded in place to a larger prefix with no disruption to running instances, which is the only non-migratory fix.

option_breakdown.A: Secondary ranges are for alias IPs, such as GKE Pods; a VM's primary internal address still comes from the full primary range.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A subnet's primary IPv4 range can be expanded in place to a larger prefix with no disruption to running instances, which is the only non-migratory fix.
option_breakdown.C: Reserving addresses takes them from the same exhausted range.
option_breakdown.D: Subnet ranges can be expanded but never shrunk, and another subnet's range wouldn't help this one.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range app-subnet \
  --region=us-central1 --prefix-length=22

questions.title: Partner has firewalled a specific address
questions.summary: Reserving the external address makes it independent of the instance lifecycle.
questions.question: An external partner's firewall allows connections only to the external IP address your VM has today, and that address must never change, even if the VM is recreated. What should you do?

options.A: Create a Cloud DNS record for the VM and give the partner the name.
options.B: Configure Cloud NAT for the VM's subnet.
options.C: Promote the VM's current external IP address to a static address.
options.D: Recreate the VM with the same name and zone whenever needed.

explanation.summary: Promoting an in-use ephemeral external IP to a static address keeps that exact address reserved, independent of the VM's lifecycle.

option_breakdown.A: The partner's firewall filters on the address, not a name.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud NAT affects outbound connections from VMs; the partner connects inbound to your VM.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A promoted static address stays reserved in the project, so a recreated VM can be given the same address.
option_breakdown.D: An ephemeral address is released when the VM is deleted; a new VM gets a different one.

questions.title: Force traffic through an appliance
questions.summary: A custom static route with the appliance's ILB as next hop overrides the default path.
questions.question: All traffic bound for the on-premises 10.50.0.0/16 range must be sent through a network virtual appliance rather than the default gateway. What should you do?

options.A: A firewall rule allowing traffic to 10.50.0.0/16 through the appliance.
options.B: Cloud NAT on the appliance's subnet.
options.C: An alias IP range of 10.50.0.0/16 on the appliance.
options.D: Add a custom static route in the VPC.

explanation.summary: A custom static route with the appliance (or its internal load balancer) as next hop overrides the default path for that destination range.

option_breakdown.A: Firewall rules allow or deny traffic; they never choose a next hop.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud NAT translates outbound internet traffic; it doesn't steer traffic to on-premises ranges.
option_breakdown.C: An alias range makes the appliance own those addresses; it doesn't send other VMs' traffic through it.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A custom static route with the appliance, or its internal load balancer, as next hop overrides the default path for that destination range.

questions.title: Private hostnames for internal services
questions.summary: A Cloud DNS private managed zone attached to the VPC serves records only to that network.
questions.question: Internal services must resolve each other by hostnames that do not exist in public DNS and must not be resolvable outside the VPC. What should you do?

options.A: A Cloud DNS private zone visible to the VPC network.
options.B: A Cloud DNS public zone with the internal names.
options.C: Entries in /etc/hosts on every VM.
options.D: Compute Engine's automatic internal DNS names.

explanation.summary: A Cloud DNS private managed zone attached to the VPC serves records only to that network, which is exactly private internal naming.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A Cloud DNS private zone attached to the VPC serves its records only to that network.
option_breakdown.B: A public zone is resolvable from anywhere on the internet.
option_breakdown.C: Hand-maintained files drift and must be updated on every VM.
option_breakdown.D: Internal DNS gives VMs names in a fixed format; it doesn't serve custom service hostnames.

questions.title: Private instances cannot reach the package mirror
questions.summary: Cloud NAT gives outbound-only internet access to instances with no external address.
questions.question: VMs in a private subnet can't reach a third-party package repository on the internet to install updates, and policy forbids external IP addresses. What should you do?

options.A: Turn on Private Google Access for the subnet.
options.B: Configure Cloud NAT on a Cloud Router.
options.C: Add a default route to the default internet gateway.
options.D: Add a firewall rule allowing egress to the repository.

explanation.summary: Cloud NAT provides outbound-only internet access for instances with no external address, satisfying both the need and the policy.

option_breakdown.A: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs and services, not a third-party repository.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud NAT gives VMs without external addresses outbound-only internet access, which meets the need and the policy.
option_breakdown.C: VMs without external IPs can't use the internet gateway on their own; the route usually exists already.
option_breakdown.D: Egress is allowed by default; the missing piece is a path out without an external IP.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute routers nats create nat-1 --router=cr-1 --region=us-central1 \
  --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

questions.title: Who talked to the compromised instance
questions.summary: VPC Flow Logs record connection records with source, destination and port.
questions.question: For the rest of an investigation, you must record which internal addresses connect to a compromised VM, and on which ports. What should you enable?

options.A: Admin Activity audit logs for Compute Engine.
options.B: Connectivity Tests in Network Intelligence Center.
options.C: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet.
options.D: Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine.

explanation.summary: VPC Flow Logs record sampled connection records with source, destination and port, which is the data this investigation needs.

option_breakdown.A: Audit logs record API calls, such as creating a VM, not network connections to it.
option_breakdown.B: Connectivity Tests analyse whether configuration allows a path; they don't record real traffic.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. VPC Flow Logs record sampled connection records with source, destination and port, which is what the investigation needs.
option_breakdown.D: Data Access logs record reads of resource data through APIs, not packets on the network.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update app-subnet --region=us-central1 \
  --enable-flow-logs --logging-flow-sampling=1.0

questions.title: Recover an overwritten object
questions.summary: Versioning keeps non-current generations of overwritten and deleted objects.
questions.question: An engineer overwrote a critical Cloud Storage object with a bad file. From now on, every earlier version of each object must stay recoverable until someone deletes it on purpose, however long ago it was overwritten. What should you enable?

options.A: Object Versioning on the bucket.
options.B: Soft delete with its longest retention period.
options.C: A daily Storage Transfer Service copy to a second bucket.
options.D: A locked retention policy on the bucket.

explanation.summary: Object versioning keeps non-current generations of overwritten and deleted objects, which is what makes this recoverable.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. With Object Versioning, an overwrite or delete keeps the previous content as a noncurrent version until it is deleted.
option_breakdown.B: Soft delete keeps overwritten and deleted objects for at most 90 days.
option_breakdown.C: A daily copy keeps only one version a day, so changes within a day are lost, and older copies are overwritten.
option_breakdown.D: It blocks every overwrite and delete during the period, including legitimate ones, rather than keeping versions.

questions.title: Records nobody can delete for five years
questions.summary: A locked bucket retention policy makes the retention period irreversible.
questions.question: Regulations require that stored records cannot be deleted by anyone — including project owners — for five years. What should you configure?

options.A: Place an object hold on each record.
options.B: Apply a bucket retention policy and lock it.
options.C: Configure an object lifecycle management rule on the bucket.
options.D: Enable object versioning on the bucket.

explanation.summary: A locked bucket retention policy makes the retention period irreversible, so even an owner cannot delete objects before it expires.

option_breakdown.A: Anyone with the right permission, project owners included, can release a hold and then delete the object.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A locked bucket retention policy makes the retention period irreversible, so even an owner cannot delete objects before it expires.
option_breakdown.C: Lifecycle rules delete or move objects; they don't stop anyone deleting them.
option_breakdown.D: Versioning keeps deleted content as noncurrent versions, but an owner can delete those too.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage buckets update gs://records --retention-period=5y
gcloud storage buckets update gs://records --lock-retention-period

questions.title: Return to the moment before a bad migration
questions.summary: Point-in-time recovery uses write-ahead logs to restore to a specific timestamp.
questions.question: A bad migration corrupted rows in a Cloud SQL database at a known time. Point-in-time recovery is enabled on the instance. The team needs the database as it was immediately before the migration ran. What should you do?

options.A: Clone the instance as it is right now, then fix the rows.
options.B: Export the database to Cloud Storage now.
options.C: Use point-in-time recovery to the moment before the migration.
options.D: Restore last night's automated backup.

explanation.summary: Point-in-time recovery uses write-ahead logs to restore to a specific timestamp, which nightly backups alone cannot do.

option_breakdown.A: A clone of the current state copies the corrupted rows.
option_breakdown.B: An export now captures the corrupted data.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Point-in-time recovery uses the instance's logs to create an instance as of a chosen timestamp, which a nightly backup alone can't.
option_breakdown.D: The backup loses every change between last night and the migration.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud sql instances clone app-db app-db-restored \
  --point-in-time='2026-08-07T14:20:00Z'

questions.title: Recover an accidentally deleted instance
questions.summary: Automated backups are restored into an instance when the original no longer exists.
questions.question: A Cloud SQL instance's data was damaged. It must be restored from its most recent automated backup into a new instance, while the damaged instance is kept for investigation. What should you do?

options.A: Clone the damaged instance.
options.B: Export the damaged instance's database to Cloud Storage.
options.C: Promote the instance's read replica.
options.D: Restore the backup to a new instance.

explanation.summary: Cloud SQL can restore a backup to a different instance, which leaves the original untouched.

option_breakdown.A: A clone copies the current, damaged data.
option_breakdown.B: An export copies the damaged data.
option_breakdown.C: A replica has the same damage, because it replicates every change.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Restoring the backup to a new instance recovers the data and keeps the damaged instance as it is.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud sql backups list --instance=app-db
gcloud sql backups restore BACKUP_ID --restore-instance=app-db-restored --backup-instance=app-db

questions.title: Hand a database copy to an external team
questions.summary: An export writes database contents to Cloud Storage as portable files.
questions.question: A copy of a Firestore database must be handed to an external analytics team as files they can load themselves. What should you do?

options.A: Export the database to Cloud Storage.
options.B: Read past data with Firestore point-in-time recovery.
options.C: Schedule Firestore backups of the database.
options.D: Grant the team Cloud Datastore Viewer on the project.

explanation.summary: An export writes the database contents to Cloud Storage as portable files, which is how data leaves the service for another consumer.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An export writes the database contents to Cloud Storage as portable files, which is how data leaves the service for another consumer.
option_breakdown.B: Point-in-time recovery lets you read or restore recent versions inside Firestore; it produces no files.
option_breakdown.C: Firestore backups can only be restored into Firestore; they aren't files someone else can load.
option_breakdown.D: That gives live access to the production database, not a copy.

questions.title: Which functions burn the CPU
questions.summary: Cloud Profiler samples the running process and attributes CPU and heap to functions.
questions.question: A single service consumes far more CPU than expected, and the team needs to know which functions inside it are responsible, in production. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Error Reporting
options.B: Active Assist recommenders
options.C: Cloud Profiler
options.D: Cloud Hub and Personalized Service Health

explanation.summary: Cloud Profiler samples the running process continuously and attributes CPU and heap to specific functions with minimal overhead.

option_breakdown.A: Error Reporting groups exceptions; high CPU needn't raise any.
option_breakdown.B: Recommenders suggest right-sizing and clean-up from usage history; they don't look inside the code.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Profiler samples the running process continuously and attributes CPU and heap to specific functions, with low overhead in production.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Hub and Service Health show incidents and application health, not which functions use CPU.

explanation.gcloud_command: # add the Cloud Profiler agent to the service; view flame graphs in the console

questions.title: Which queries are loading the database
questions.summary: Query Insights attributes database load to normalised queries and tags their origin.
questions.question: A Cloud SQL instance shows sustained high load, and the team must identify which queries and which application hosts are causing it. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Cloud Hub and Personalized Service Health
options.B: Cloud Trace
options.C: Cloud Profiler
options.D: Query Insights

explanation.summary: Query Insights attributes database load to normalised queries and tags them with the originating application, which is precisely this question.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud Hub shows incidents and health across applications, not which queries load a database.
option_breakdown.B: Trace shows slow spans in requests that are traced; it doesn't rank the database's load by query.
option_breakdown.C: Profiler looks inside application processes, not inside the database.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Query Insights attributes database load to normalised queries and, with application tags, to the hosts and code that send them.

questions.title: Which VMs are idle or oversized
questions.summary: Active Assist recommenders emit idle-resource and right-sizing recommendations.
questions.question: Finance asks which VMs are idle and which machine types are oversized, so they can be removed or resized to cut the bill. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Active Assist recommenders
options.B: Cloud Profiler
options.C: Query Insights
options.D: CPU dashboards in Cloud Monitoring, reviewed by hand.

explanation.summary: Active Assist recommenders analyse usage and emit idle-resource and machine-type right-sizing recommendations, which is exactly this request.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Active Assist recommenders analyse usage and produce idle-VM and machine-type right-sizing recommendations.
option_breakdown.B: Profiler looks inside one application's code, not across the fleet's VMs.
option_breakdown.C: Query Insights is about database queries, not VM sizing.
option_breakdown.D: Dashboards show usage, but someone would have to judge every VM by hand, and memory isn't on them by default.

questions.title: Deduplicated view of application exceptions
questions.summary: Error Reporting groups stack traces into distinct errors with counts and first-seen times.
questions.question: The team wants a deduplicated view of which exceptions occur most often and when each first appeared, rather than searching raw logs. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Active Assist recommenders
options.B: Error Reporting
options.C: Cloud Hub and Personalized Service Health
options.D: Cloud Trace

explanation.summary: Error Reporting groups stack traces into distinct errors with counts and first-seen timestamps, which raw log searching does not.

option_breakdown.A: Recommenders suggest optimisations; they don't group exceptions.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Error Reporting groups stack traces into distinct errors with counts and first-seen times, which searching raw logs doesn't give.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Hub shows incidents and health, not individual exceptions.
option_breakdown.D: Trace shows latency per request, not grouped exceptions.

questions.title: One view of incidents affecting our projects
questions.summary: Cloud Hub and Personalized Service Health aggregate events and health per project.
questions.question: An operations lead wants one place to see active Google Cloud incidents that affect their own projects, plus the health of their applications across the estate. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Cloud Trace
options.B: Cloud Profiler
options.C: Cloud Hub and Personalized Service Health
options.D: Query Insights

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub aggregates active events and application health across the estate, and Personalized Service Health surfaces the Google Cloud incidents that actually affect your projects.

option_breakdown.A: Trace shows latency inside your requests, not Google Cloud incidents.
option_breakdown.B: Profiler shows CPU and memory by function, not incidents or application health.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Hub shows application health across the estate, and Personalized Service Health shows the Google Cloud incidents that affect your projects.
option_breakdown.D: Query Insights is about database query load only.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud Hub; Console > Service Health for personalised incidents

questions.title: Disable the key to render data unreadable
questions.summary: CMEK puts key lifecycle under your control, so disabling it makes protected data unreadable.
questions.question: Policy requires that the organisation be able to disable the key protecting a BigQuery dataset, rendering the data unreadable on demand. What should you configure?

options.A: Rely on Google-managed encryption keys, applied by default.
options.B: Configure customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS.
options.C: Supply customer-supplied encryption keys with each request.
options.D: Revoke every IAM grant on the dataset when needed.

explanation.summary: CMEK puts the key lifecycle under your control, so disabling or destroying the key makes the protected data unreadable — something Google-managed keys cannot offer.

option_breakdown.A: Google manages default keys; you can't disable them to make one dataset unreadable.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. CMEK puts the key lifecycle under your control, so disabling or destroying the key makes the protected data unreadable — something Google-managed keys cannot offer.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery doesn't accept customer-supplied keys; CSEK applies to Cloud Storage and Compute Engine.
option_breakdown.D: Anyone with IAM rights can grant access again, and the data itself stays readable; this isn't cryptographic revocation.

questions.title: FIPS 140-2 Level 3 key material
questions.summary: The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement.
questions.question: A regulator requires that key material be generated and used only inside a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security module. What should you configure?

options.A: Supply customer-supplied encryption keys with each API request.
options.B: Use a Cloud KMS key with the SOFTWARE protection level.
options.C: Use a Cloud KMS key with the HSM protection level.
options.D: Rely on Google-managed encryption keys, applied by default.

explanation.summary: The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement, which software-protected keys do not.

option_breakdown.A: With CSEK you hold the keys, but Google still uses them in its own systems; you get no validated HSM for them.
option_breakdown.B: Software keys are validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 1, not Level 3.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The HSM protection level in Cloud KMS meets that certification requirement, which software-protected keys do not.
option_breakdown.D: Default keys are managed entirely by Google, with no HSM requirement you can set.

questions.title: Store a database password centrally
questions.summary: Secret Manager stores versioned secret values with per-secret IAM.
questions.question: A database password used by an application must be stored centrally, versioned, and readable only by that application's service account. What should you use?

options.A: An environment variable in the instance template.
options.B: A custom metadata value on the application's VMs.
options.C: Ciphertext encrypted with Cloud KMS, committed to the repository.
options.D: Store the value in Secret Manager.

explanation.summary: Secret Manager is the managed store for exactly this: versioned secret values with per-secret IAM.

option_breakdown.A: Anyone who can view the template can read it, and it isn't versioned on its own.
option_breakdown.B: Any process on the VM, and anyone who can view the instance, can read metadata.
option_breakdown.C: Every clone of the repository holds the secret, and rotating it means a commit; there's no per-secret access control.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Secret Manager stores versioned secret values, and an IAM grant on the secret lets only the application's service account read it.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud secrets create db-password --replication-policy=automatic
gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password \
  --member='serviceAccount:app@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com' \
  --role='roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor'

questions.title: What must be configured for encryption at rest
questions.summary: All data at rest is encrypted by default; no configuration is needed absent a key-control requirement.
questions.question: A team asks what they must configure to encrypt Cloud Storage data at rest. They have no requirement to control or revoke the key themselves. What should you tell them?

options.A: Rely on Google-managed encryption keys, applied by default.
options.B: Use a Cloud KMS key with the HSM protection level.
options.C: Store the value in Secret Manager.
options.D: Configure customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS.

explanation.summary: All data at rest in Google Cloud is encrypted by default with Google-managed keys, so no configuration is required when there is no key-control requirement.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. All data at rest in Google Cloud is encrypted by default with Google-managed keys, so no configuration is required when there is no key-control requirement.
option_breakdown.B: An HSM key adds cost and key management for control nobody asked for.
option_breakdown.C: Secret Manager stores secrets such as passwords; it doesn't encrypt buckets.
option_breakdown.D: CMEK adds key management they don't need, since there is no requirement to control the key.

questions.title: Rotate the disk key every 90 days
questions.summary: A Cloud KMS key with a rotation period is a CMEK capability; managed keys expose no schedule.
questions.question: Compliance requires that the key protecting Persistent Disks be rotated every 90 days on an automatic schedule under the customer's control. What should you configure?

options.A: Rotate the Google-managed encryption keys every 90 days from the console.
options.B: Create the disks with a Cloud KMS key that has a 90-day rotation period (CMEK).
options.C: Supply a new customer-supplied encryption key with each disk operation every 90 days.
options.D: Re-create every disk every 90 days so it gets a new default key.

explanation.summary: A Cloud KMS key's rotation period creates a new primary version on schedule, under the customer's control, and Compute Engine uses it for new encryption.

option_breakdown.A: Google-managed keys are rotated by Google; the customer has no rotation setting to control.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A Cloud KMS key's rotation period creates a new primary version on schedule, under the customer's control, and Compute Engine uses it for new encryption.
option_breakdown.C: CSEK has no schedule: you would rotate and supply raw keys yourself on every call.
option_breakdown.D: Re-creating disks is disruptive and still leaves the key under Google's control.

questions.title: Every externally exposed Service in a cluster
questions.summary: kubectl get services --all-namespaces lists every Service with its type and external IP.
questions.question: During a security review, you must list every Kubernetes Service in a GKE cluster that has an external IP address, whatever namespace it is in. What should you list?

options.A: The Pods, with their IP addresses and nodes.
options.B: The Services in every namespace.
options.C: The GKE cluster's own description.
options.D: The nodes, with their external IP addresses.

explanation.summary: Services carry the TYPE and EXTERNAL-IP columns; --all-namespaces (-A) removes the namespace scope. LoadBalancer Services with an address in EXTERNAL-IP are the ones exposed.

option_breakdown.A: Pod listings show Pod IPs and nodes, not how workloads are exposed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubectl get services --all-namespaces lists Services across every namespace with their external IPs.
option_breakdown.C: The cluster description covers cluster settings, not the Services inside it.
option_breakdown.D: Node external IPs are not how applications are exposed and miss every load balancer.

questions.title: Which node and node pool each Pod runs on
questions.summary: kubectl get pods -o wide shows each Pod's node; node labels show the node pool.
questions.question: You need to know which node each Pod of the 'payments' namespace is running on, and which node pool those nodes belong to. What should you run?

options.A: A description of the payments Deployment.
options.B: The cluster's list of node pools.
options.C: Pods with their nodes, then nodes with their pool label.
options.D: The Pods' current resource usage.

explanation.summary: The wide output adds a NODE column per Pod; GKE labels every node with cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, which -L displays as a column. Together they map Pods to nodes to pools.

option_breakdown.A: A Deployment description shows the template and rollout, not placement per Pod.
option_breakdown.B: Lists pools but not which Pods run on their nodes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. kubectl get pods -o wide gives each Pod's node, and kubectl get nodes -L cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool gives each node's pool.
option_breakdown.D: Shows resource usage, not placement.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl get pods -n payments -o wide
kubectl get nodes -L cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool

questions.title: An Autopilot Pod killed for memory
questions.summary: Autopilot provisions capacity from each container's requests; raise the memory request to give the Pod more.
questions.question: A container on a GKE Autopilot cluster is repeatedly OOMKilled. Its manifest sets a memory request of 512Mi and no other resource values. The application genuinely needs about 1.5 GiB. What should you change?

options.A: Add a node pool with larger machines to the cluster.
options.B: Remove the memory request so Autopilot can allocate memory dynamically.
options.C: Enable the cluster autoscaler on the Autopilot cluster.
options.D: Raise the container's memory request to about 1.5Gi.

explanation.summary: Autopilot sizes capacity, and bills, from Pod resource requests, and applies limits based on them. The fix is a request that matches real usage. Node pools and the cluster autoscaler are managed by Google in Autopilot.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot manages nodes; you do not add node pools.
option_breakdown.B: Without a request Autopilot applies a small default, which makes the problem worse.
option_breakdown.C: Node scaling is automatic in Autopilot and is not the constraint here.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The request is what Autopilot allocates and bills.

questions.title: A canary split for a Cloud Run function
questions.summary: Cloud Run functions are Cloud Run services, so traffic is split between their revisions with update-traffic.
questions.question: A function deployed with `gcloud functions deploy` (Cloud Run functions) has a new version. You want 20% of requests to reach the new revision and 80% the previous one. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the new version as a second function and weight the two URLs in Cloud DNS.
options.B: Put both versions behind an external Application Load Balancer with weighted backends.
options.C: Delete the old revision so the platform shifts traffic gradually by itself.
options.D: Split traffic between the function's revisions.

explanation.summary: A Cloud Run function is deployed as a Cloud Run service, so it has revisions and supports percentage traffic splits and tags exactly like any other Cloud Run service.

option_breakdown.A: DNS weighting is coarse, cached by clients, and doubles what you operate.
option_breakdown.B: A load balancer is unnecessary; the service already splits traffic between revisions.
option_breakdown.C: Deleting the previous revision removes the rollback target and does not create a gradual split.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Revision-level percentages on the underlying Cloud Run service.

questions.title: Weighted routing between two versions on GKE
questions.summary: With the Gateway API, an HTTPRoute's backendRefs weights split traffic between Services.
questions.question: On GKE, version 1 and version 2 of an application run as separate Deployments, each behind its own Service, exposed through the Gateway API. You want 90% of requests on v1 and 10% on v2. What should you change?

options.A: Scale v1 to nine replicas and v2 to one, relying on one Service selecting both.
options.B: Weights of 90 and 10 on the HTTPRoute's two backends.
options.C: Create a second Gateway for v2 and give users its IP address.
options.D: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to v2 with a 10% CPU target.

explanation.summary: An HTTPRoute can reference several backend Services with weights, and GKE's Gateway controller programs the load balancer to split traffic accordingly — independent of replica counts.

option_breakdown.A: Replica ratios give only approximate splits and couple capacity to routing.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Precise, declarative weights at the load balancer.
option_breakdown.C: A separate entry point means clients choose the version, not a percentage split.
option_breakdown.D: An autoscaler changes replica counts; it does not route traffic.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f route.yaml   # HTTPRoute backendRefs: [{name: app-v1, weight: 90}, {name: app-v2, weight: 10}]

questions.title: Adding a GPU to an existing VM
questions.summary: Attaching a GPU requires the VM to be stopped, host maintenance set to TERMINATE, and the GPU offered in its zone.
questions.question: An existing N1 VM needs an NVIDIA T4 attached for an inference workload. What must be true for the change to succeed?

options.A: It is stopped, set to terminate on maintenance, and T4s exist in its zone.
options.B: It keeps running; GPUs hot-plug and the maintenance policy can stay.
options.C: It is converted to Spot, since GPUs are offered only as Spot capacity.
options.D: It is recreated in any region, since GPUs are global resources.

explanation.summary: GPUs cannot live-migrate, so an instance with GPUs must use onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE. The accelerator is attached while the VM is stopped, and only GPU models offered in the VM's zone (and compatible with its machine series) can be attached.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. All three conditions apply to attaching a GPU to an existing instance.
option_breakdown.B: GPUs are not hot-plugged, and live migration is not supported for them.
option_breakdown.C: GPUs are available on standard as well as Spot provisioning.
